run.question:
1. List the tables in the database and tell me the verification code from the holmes_eval_222 table
2. I'm experiencing slow queries with this SQL: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345
   Analyze why this query is slow and suggest how to fix it

report.summary: The configured ClickHouse database (target m0-otel-20260909, schema default) contains exactly two tables: holmes_eval_222 and orders (fact). holmes_eval_222 holds one row (id 1, category eval_test) whose verification_code is HOLMES-CLICKHOUSE-EVAL-222-v5t8n2 (fact). For the slow-query question: the SELECT is syntactically valid ClickHouse, but orders has its primary key and sorting key on id only, with zero data-skipping indices, so a predicate on customer_id cannot prune anything — EXPLAIN indexes=1 shows 'PrimaryKey Condition: true, Parts 1/1, Granules 1/1' and my instrumented COUNT with the same customer_id predicate read all 10,000 rows (40,000 bytes). That full-scan behaviour is a supported fact and is the plausible mechanism for slow queries as data grows (hypothesis). However, slowness was NOT observed here: the table currently holds 10,000 rows in a single part (139.40 KiB), every query in system.query_log ran in ≤9 ms, and customer_id = 12345 matches 0 rows because customer_id values only span 1..1000 in this dataset — so the stated symptom is unverified at this data size, and the test predicate is out of range. Recommendations are advisory only; nothing was changed.

claims.text: The configured ClickHouse database lists two tables, both in schema default: holmes_eval_222 and orders.

Table holmes_eval_222 has columns id, category, verification_code, created_at and returns exactly one row: id=1, category='eval_test', verification_code='HOLMES-CLICKHOUSE-EVAL-222-v5t8n2', created_at='2026-11-22 10:09:29'.

Table orders has columns id UInt32, customer_id UInt32, order_date Date, total_amount Decimal(10,2), status String; its primary key is [id] and its only index is a sorting_key on id (no index or key includes customer_id).

EXPLAIN indexes = 1 for 'SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345' shows ReadFromMergeTree (default.orders) with PrimaryKey Condition: true and Parts 1/1, Granules 1/1, i.e. the customer_id predicate provides no key-based pruning and all granules are read.

An equivalent executed query, 'SELECT count(*) AS matching_rows FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345', read 10,000 rows and 40,000 bytes (full scan of the customer_id column) and completed in 2 ms per system.query_log; its result was 0 matching rows.

orders currently holds 10,000 rows in 1 active part totalling 139.40 KiB, with 1000 distinct customer_id values; customer_id ranges from 1 to 1000 and id from 0 to 9999, so customer_id = 12345 lies outside the data and matches nothing.

system.query_log for the last 2 days shows no slow statements: the slowest entry is the 9 ms bulk INSERT that populated orders at 2026-11-22 10:09:29, and the customer_id-filtered SELECTs run in 2-3 ms; the table and its data were created at 2026-11-22 10:09:28-10:09:29, i.e. within minutes of this query.

The structural reason this query scales badly as orders grows is that the primary key/sorting key is id only and there are no data-skipping indices or verified projections on customer_id, so every execution scans every row/granule and, with SELECT *, reads all columns rather than pruning by the filter column; this is a plausible cause of slowness at larger data volumes but was not observed as slowness in this 10,000-row dataset.

Rejected as this dataset's explanation: that an established, heavily loaded orders table is producing slow customer_id lookups. The table has 1 part / 10,000 rows / 139.40 KiB, the filtered query returned 0 rows and took 2 ms, and no slow statement exists in the 2-day query_log window I sampled.

Give the filter column a key path: define the table with ORDER BY (customer_id, order_date, id) (or ORDER BY (customer_id, id) for point lookups) when re-creating/re-populating it, so predicates on customer_id can prune granules; use an explicit column list instead of SELECT * so only needed columns are read.

If the table cannot be re-keyed, add a skipping index or projection on customer_id, e.g. ALTER TABLE orders ADD INDEX idx_customer_id customer_id TYPE minmax GRANULARITY 1 (low selectivity, weak) or TYPE bloom_filter GRANULARITY 1, or ALTER TABLE orders ADD PROJECTION p_customer (SELECT * ORDER BY customer_id) and MATERIALIZE it — these are proposals only and were not executed; verify with EXPLAIN indexes = 1 that Condition changes from 'true' to a real predicate.

Validate the workload against real data before acting: customer_id = 12345 matches nothing in this dataset (values 1..1000) and there is no observed slow history, so confirm real row counts, the actual production predicate values and measured query durations (system.query_log, query_duration_ms) before changing schema.

gaps: No observed slow execution of this statement: system.query_log for the last 2 days contains only queries from 2026-11-22 10:09:28-10:09:55, all ≤9 ms, and the dataset was created minutes before this investigation, so historical production latency is unknown.
Query text is not tied to any application service: I did not find evidence of which client issues 'SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ...', so end-user or downstream impact is unverified.

Projection coverage could not be checked: querying `system`.projections failed with error 60 (UNKNOWN_TABLE, Table system.projections does not exist) and SHOW CREATE TABLE orders was refused as a non-read-only construct, so any projections defined on orders are unknown.
system.query_log retention/completeness for the authorized window is not guaranteed; a statement absent from it may simply have aged out or not been captured.
The change_history integration is not available in this Run, so no change/DDL history for the orders schema or its data load could be reviewed.
Secret values were not needed and cannot be read; nothing in this conclusion depends on a secret, but no secret-backed connection parameters were verified.
next_steps: Have the application owner capture the real slow statement's query_duration_ms, read_rows and read_bytes from system.query_log on the production scale table.
Ask the DBA to review the production orders DDL (sorting key, projections, skipping indices) and confirm row count and customer_id cardinality.
If confirmed, plan a schema change to ORDER BY (customer_id, ...) or a projection on customer_id, and measure before/after with EXPLAIN indexes = 1 and system.query_log durations.
